title: From Bridge To Pioneer: Digital Fashion With Clo [✨En/Jp Subtitles Provided]
description:
Jaeyong Lee (founder of VGlab), a pioneer in 3D fashion education, is redefining what’s possible for individual designers and students using CLO. Beyond accelerating Paris Fashion Week production with ANREALAGE, he has established new technical standards specifically for the CLO community:  
- Accelerated runway production by 80%, condensing a traditional 6-month sample cycle into just 5 weeks.  
- Developed and open-sourced a proprietary CLO-to-Blender integration plugin, streamlining complex animation pipelines for global 3D artists.

"I am bridging the gap between physical reality and digital creation, empowering designers to express their ultimate creativity without technical constraints. CLO doesn't just speed up production; it redefines the entire lifestyle of modern fashion design." by Jaeyong Lee

transcript: Hello, my name is Lee Jae-yong and I work for the SNS brand called Tokyo Yubunan. We run a studio called V-Grab in Tokyo. We mainly produce fashion and digital content for apparel brands that use black 3D and 3D CG. I first met black in 2018 when I was a teacher at the Faculty of Arts and Sciences. At that time, there was no one in the school who knew black. So I started to study by myself while teaching students. It was seven or eight years ago. I had the opportunity to see the user story of the Italian bike wear Dainese. I was very impressed that it could already be used in real life. Seeing that, I wanted to be a creator who uses 3D in the apparel field, so I started to study deeply. After graduating from the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, I wanted to become a professional designer. While studying CG exclusively, I heard from a friend that a brand like Unreal Engine would be interested in it. I had the opportunity to show the results online. The COVID-19 pandemic began about a month to two months later. At that time, I hurriedly got a call from Mr. Morinaga and asked if digital sampling was possible. I thought that black 3D was an important opportunity to apply for a real job. I thought I could do it quickly. I was surprised. When I came to see this product, I was able to make it. I had no idea how to make a 3D video in a fashion world. I had no one to translate.... So we couldn't do it. At first I thought that I would not be able to create something like this on the scale of this cuando. But after all, the gap is almost gone. The production period is six months. I was able to reduce what took about half a year to a month. I felt that what I drew on the screen and what was actually born were almost the same. I felt a lot of potential there. He knows the structure of clothes well. At the same time, he knew a lot about black and 3D at the same level. With that translation, I realized that I could make so many things virtually. I think that the difference between the real fashion and the virtual fashion is getting less and less. There may be some ups and downs in the future, but I think that the virtual fashion will continue to grow. I think that the virtual fashion will continue to grow. I think that the virtual fashion will continue to grow. I think that the virtual fashion will continue to grow. I don't know what will happen, but I'm sure that the world of both worlds is expanding. If I can't express myself in 3D, I think I'll have to stop the idea of a designer. I work with the idea that I have to express myself in any form. As I continue to work with multiple brands, I started to think that it's necessary to have a company to stay on top of the business. I started a V-grab where fashion and technology connect. I have the most memorable collection called Dimension in the SS in 2022. It was a collaboration project with Mamoru Hosoda's director Ryu and Sobakatsu Hime. It was a very tight schedule. It was a project where I had to verify the actual collection piece and produce the data for the TG for the costume. It was a project where I had to verify the actual collection piece and produce the data for the costume for the TG for the costume. I think it was possible because it was a 3D-based project. Qrow is a tool that doesn't have many self-made plugins compared to other 3D tools. I use Qrow and Blender, but I made a plugin that sends data in one click. I thought that other workers would also need it, so I released it in open source. For me, Qrow is a language that allows me to put what I imagine into the world. Blender already has an MCP that connects to AI, but Qrow doesn't. So I'm developing an MCP for Qrow. It's still a test version, but I'm looking forward to the possibility of controlling Qrow with AI. The power of designers to think in 3D and express themselves will come in the era of fashion's basic literacy. I think it will expand the actual limit and lead to a speedy collaboration. I want V-Grab to play a good role in that flow. I'm looking forward to working with V-Grab in the future, so I'm looking forward to working with V-Grab in the future.
markdown_content: ## Company Background: Tokyo Yubunan and V-Grab in Digital Fashion This section introduces Lee Jae-yong, his role at Tokyo Yubunan, and the studio V-Grab’s focus on digital apparel production using black 3D and 3D CG. It also frames his long-term goal of making virtual fashion feel closer to real fashion. - **Name/Role:** Lee Jae-yong - **Company/Brand:** **Tokyo Yubunan** (SNS brand) - **Studio:** **V-Grab** (based in Tokyo) - **Primary work:** Producing **fashion and digital content** for apparel brands using **black 3D** and **3D CG**. ## Learning Black 3D from 2018: From Self-Study to Real-World Inspiration This section explains how Lee began studying black 3D in **2018**, initially as a teacher, and how seeing industry use cases pushed him to pursue 3D for apparel. It includes the motivation derived from a real brand’s “user story.” - **2018:** Lee encountered **black** while working as a **teacher at the Faculty of Arts and Sciences**. - At the time, **no one at the school knew black**, so he began **studying independently** while teaching students. - **7–8 years ago (time reference):** He reviewed the **user story of the Italian bike wear brand Dainese** and was impressed that the technology could be used in **real life**. - Motivated by this, he aimed to become a **3D creator in the apparel field** and “studied deeply.” - After graduating, he wanted to become a **professional designer**. ## Transition to Professional CG: Unreal Engine Interest and Online Showcasing This section describes Lee’s shift from CG study to professional exposure, including hearing about **Unreal Engine**, showing results online, and the career opportunity that followed. - While studying **CG exclusively**, a friend suggested that a brand like **Unreal Engine** might be interested. - Lee had the opportunity to **show the results online**. - The **COVID-19 pandemic** began about **one to two months later**, changing the pace of his career path. ## Digital Sampling During COVID-19: Request, Production, and Timeline Reduction This section covers the COVID-era turning point: a call from **Mr. Morinaga**, a request to determine whether **digital sampling** was possible, and the resulting production improvements. It also includes key production duration details. - During early COVID-19, Lee received a hurried call from **Mr. Morinaga** asking if **digital sampling** was possible. - Lee viewed **black 3D** as an important opportunity to secure a real job and believed he could respond quickly. - He was surprised by the outcome: after visiting/seeing the product, he was able to produce it. - He noted he had **no prior knowledge of how to make a 3D video in the fashion world**, and lacked translation/support, which initially made it difficult to proceed. - He first thought producing something at the required **scale** would be difficult, but the gap decreased significantly. - **Production period:** **six months** (as the baseline timeframe he mentions). - He reduced the time from roughly **half a year to about a month**. - He observed a strong match between **what was drawn on screen** and **what was actually created**, leading him to feel the process had “a lot of potential.” ## Why Virtual Fashion Is Closing the Gap: Structure, Rendering, and Collaboration Potential This section explains Lee’s belief that virtual fashion is becoming closer to real fashion. It connects success to understanding clothing structure and equal proficiency in black and 3D, and it discusses future growth and expansion. - Lee emphasizes that success depends on both: - Knowing the **structure of clothes** well. - Knowing **black and 3D** at the same level. - With that “translation,” he realized many things can be made **virtually**. - He believes the difference between **real fashion** and **virtual fashion** is **getting less and less**. - He expects some future **ups and downs**, but believes **virtual fashion will continue to grow**. - He frames the future as the expansion of “the world of both worlds.” - If he cannot express himself in 3D, he believes he would have to stop thinking of himself as a designer—because he works with the principle that expression must be possible **in any form**. ## Building V-Grab: Connecting Fashion and Technology for Ongoing Business This section describes why Lee started V-Grab—his growing realization that he needed a company to keep up with business—and how V-Grab positions itself at the intersection of fashion and technology. - As he worked with **multiple brands**, he concluded it was necessary to have a company to remain on top of the business. - He started **V-Grab**, explicitly positioning it as a place where **fashion and technology connect**. ## Signature Collection (SS 2022): Dimension Collaboration and TG Costume Data This section details Lee’s most memorable collection, **Dimension** (SS 2022), describing the collaboration, schedule pressure, and the technical requirement to verify real pieces and generate TG costume data. - **Most memorable collection:** **Dimension** - **Season:** **SS 2022** - **Collaboration:** With **Mamoru Hosoda** (director **Ryu**) and **Sobakatsu Hime**. - **Schedule:** “Very tight.” - **Technical requirements:** - **Verify the actual collection pieces**. - Produce **data for the TG for the costume**. - The repeated emphasis suggests the project relied on **3D-based production** to make that workflow feasible. ## Tools and Workflow: Qrow, Blender, and One-Click Data Export Plugin This section explains Lee’s toolchain—**Qrow and Blender**—and the reason he built and released an open-source plugin. It includes the specific functionality: one-click data sending. - Lee notes **Qrow** has **fewer self-made plugins** than other 3D tools. - He uses **Qrow and Blender**. - He created a **plugin** that **sends data in one click**. - He released the plugin as **open source**, believing other workers would also need it. ## AI Integration: MCP for Qrow and Future AI-Controlled 3D Work This section covers Lee’s view of Qrow as a “language” for imagination, explains Blender’s existing MCP-to-AI connectivity, and describes his development of an MCP for Qrow (currently a test version) to enable AI control. - Lee describes **Qrow** as a “language” that lets him put what he imagines into the world. - He states that **Blender already has an MCP** that connects to AI, but **Qrow does not**. - He is **developing an MCP for Qrow**. - Status: the MCP is **still a test version**. - Goal: the possibility of **controlling Qrow with AI**. ## Future Outlook: 3D Literacy as Fashion’s “Basic Literacy” This section summarizes Lee’s forward-looking belief that designers’ ability to think in 3D will become a kind of foundational literacy for fashion. It ties this to faster collaboration and V-Grab’s role. - Lee believes the power of designers to **think in 3D** and express themselves will grow in the era of **fashion’s basic literacy**. - He expects this to: - Expand the “actual limit.” - Lead to **speedy collaboration**. - He wants **V-Grab** to play a good role in this flow and looks forward to continuing work with V-Grab.
